title: Whole-body manipulation runs untethered on Thor-class compute by H1 2027
body: By H1 2027, at least one humanoid-robot vendor or lab will publicly demonstrate or report a whole-body manipulation policy — one that coordinates legs, waist, arms, head, and end-effectors to handle objects while the robot is still moving — running entirely on the machine's own onboard compute, untethered from any external workstation. The precondition landed on July 13, 2026, when Booster Robotics launched Booster T2, whose Pro edition mounts NVIDIA's flagship Thor module rated at up to 2,070 TFLOPS — which Booster bills as the most powerful compute yet carried by any bipedal humanoid — paired with an open development ecosystem. This matters because the humanoid field has moved its bar from clean bipedal walking to whole-body manipulation under vision-language-action policies — learned models that map camera input and a language instruction directly to motor actions — and the gating problem has been where that policy runs: today's manipulation work frequently streams perception to, and takes actions from, a tethered workstation, because the neural policy is too heavy to execute at control-loop rates on the robot itself. Putting Thor-class compute — on the order of 2,000 TFLOPS — physically on the robot removes that tether as a hardware constraint, and a shipping developer platform at that compute tier lowers the barrier for the labs building manipulation skills. With multiple vendors now competing on exactly this ground and an open ecosystem inviting outside labs to build on T2, the first public, documented instance of whole-body manipulation executed on onboard Thor-class silicon rather than a workstation is the natural next milestone. The landing condition: by H1 2027, at least one humanoid vendor or lab publicly reports — in a demo, technical writeup, or deployment — a whole-body manipulation task executed with the policy running fully on the robot's onboard Thor-class compute, explicitly untethered from an external workstation.

reasoning.because: Booster T2 Pro carries NVIDIA's Thor module onboard, rated up to 2,070 TFLOPS of on-robot compute
reasoning.given: Bar moved to whole-body manipulation; on-robot vs. tethered-workstation policy execution is the gate
reasoning.so_that: ≥1 humanoid vendor publicly reports a whole-body manipulation task run fully on onboard Thor-class compute, untethered
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; ≥1 humanoid vendor/lab via public demo, post, or deployment writeup
reasoning.plain_language: Right now robot hands often rely on a nearby plugged-in computer. Soon a robot will do full-body handling using only the brain inside it.

summary: Booster's T2 Pro humanoid carries an NVIDIA Thor module rated up to 2,070 TFLOPS onboard. Because running whole-body manipulation on the robot rather than a tethered workstation is the gating problem, expect at least one vendor to report it executed fully on onboard Thor-class compute by H1 2027.
